description: Two weeks after I bought it, this company printed an all-time record, raised guidance for the second time this year, and hit its 2028 targets two years early. The market marked it down.
body_html:
Table of Contents

  • The position, and the number that matters

  • TLDR

  • How the company ranks

  • The quarter, decomposed

  • The scorecard: what I got right, and what I got wrong

  • Thesis scorecard after Q2 2026

  • The guidance raise, and the second half nobody believes

  • Valuation: what changed in the model

  • Risk register update

  • Where the company sits against its peers

  • Verdict

The position, and the number that matters

On 15 July I put 3.5% of the portfolio into Constellium [], at $28.98 a share, and published the deep dive the next day. Two weeks later the company reported the best quarter in its history, raised full-year guidance for the second time in 2026, and delivered the profit and cash flow targets it had promised for 2028, two years ahead of schedule.

The stock fell 6% that day. It trades at $28.42 today, 1.9% below my cost, and the model says it is worth more than twice that.

Everything that follows argues the other direction. Since 6 July the model’s value has gone up and the price has gone down. That is the whole update in one sentence.

TLDR

  • Q2 2026 Segment Adjusted EBITDA of $310M ex metal-price lag, an all-time record, +88% y/y, with simultaneous quarterly records at A&T and P&ARP. Diluted GAAP EPS of $1.04 against $0.25 a year ago.

  • Shipments fell 1%. Every dollar of the increase came from price, mix and cost, not volume.

  • Guidance raised a second time: 2026 Adjusted EBITDA ex lag from $900M-$940M to $980M-$1.020B, FCF from above $275M to above $300M. That delivers the 2028 targets in 2026.

  • Leverage 1.8x, down from 3.5x a year ago. $100M of the 2028 notes redeemed early in July. $20M of stock bought back in the quarter.

  • Of my five thesis pillars, four are confirmed and one is unchanged. Nothing is challenged. But I got four forecasts wrong, and I show them below.

  • Model target moves $60 to $62 on the new guidance, bear case unchanged at $20. At $28.35 that is +119% upside against 29% downside, an R/R of 1 to 4.0. Maintaining BUY.

  • RankedStocks now scores CSTM 92, up from 83 at the deep dive, and 99th percentile globally. Profitability went 34 to 85 and Growth 32 to 62 as the trough quarters rolled out of the trailing window.

How the company ranks

Four weeks ago CSTM scored 83 on RankedStocks with a very particular shape: near-perfect forward-looking factors (Sentiment & Outlook) against depressed trailing ones (Growth & Profitability). I argued that shape was the thesis, in quantitative form. The backward-looking scores described the old company; the forward-looking ones described the company management was running.

Q2 has started closing that gap.

Profitability 34 to 85. The largest single move. Every margin metric scores badly from gross margin, EBITDA margin to net margin. Every return metric scores superbly: from ROE, asset turnover, return on total capital to ROIC.

That is the same denominator effect I deal with in the valuation section further down. Margins look thin because revenue is inflated by metal the company buys and passes straight through at no markup; returns look excellent because the capital actually employed to convert that metal is modest. On a pass-through business, the return metrics are the honest ones.

On a trailing basis, group EBITDA of $888M sits just below the $992M record set in the twelve months to Q1 2022, and it is climbing.

Trailing net income has already cleared its own record, at $546M against a prior peak near $400M, and against $34M a year ago.

This is what I meant when I wrote that the score would improve as the trough quarters rolled out of the data.

Growth 32 to 62. The trailing metrics are already excellent: diluted EPS growth, ROE growth, ROIC growth, EBIT growth. What holds the composite down to 62 is the forward column. Consensus forward EPS growth, and forward long-term EPS growth. Revenue growth y/y is still negative, which is the shipment story rather than a demand story. So this is not a stale trailing window catching up. It is the Street forecasting that this year’s earnings shrink from here.

Valuation 51 to 70. The stock got cheaper on a trailing basis, because earnings rose while the price fell. Every earnings and cash-flow multiple screens cheap: 7.0x trailing earnings, 6.4x forward earnings, 5.2x trailing EV/EBITDA, 5.4x forward, 0.6x EV/sales.

What stops the factor from reaching the high eighties is a different family of measures entirely: a price-to-book of 3.0x, an EV/IC of 2.3x, and a zero dividend yield. Two of those three are legacies of the decade this thesis is about. Book equity was negative as recently as 2016 and has only just been rebuilt, and the absent dividend is a choice in favour of buybacks. On the measures that reflect what the business earns today, this is one of the cheapest names in its sector.

Both sentiment (96 → 88) and outlook (98 → 96) slipped. These are the forward-looking factors, and they softened slightly even as the company beat and raised. That is the market pricing the second-half taper, and I address it directly further down.

The composite went to 92 and the percentile ranking to 99. The interesting part is that the improvement came almost entirely from the trailing factors catching up to reality, while the forward factors gave a little back. The re-rating I described as half-finished is still half-finished; it just moved from the numerator to the denominator.

Sixty-two days in the Elite band now. The price chart underneath it shows the round trip: up 70% from February to the early-June high near $36, then a slide back to $28 while the fundamentals improved.

You can run this framework on any ticker yourself, for free, at RankedStocks.com.

The quarter, decomposed

In Q2 2026, revenue rose 31% y/y and beat consensus estimate (8th quarter in a row).

Net income was $148M against $36M. Diluted GAAP EPS was $1.04 against $0.25, beating the $0.86 consensus by 21%.

Adjusted EBITDA was $439M, but that number includes a positive non-cash metal price lag of $129M, and I strip it, as does management. The figure that matters is Segment Adjusted EBITDA of $310M, an all-time record and +88% y/y.

Shipments went down 1%. Every dollar of that $145M increase in segment profit came from price, mix and cost. This is a business that made 88% more money on 1% less volume. For a converter, that is either a very good sign about pricing power or a very good sign about the cost environment, and the honest answer is that it is both, in a mix I will separate below.

A&T set a quarterly record up 61%. Shipments rose 21%, with aerospace up 14% and transportation, industry and defence up 26%. The majority of the EBITDA contribution came from volume and to a lesser degree from price & mix partially offset by cost. Segment EBITDA per tonne hit $2,083, the first time the segment has crossed $2,000.

This is the segment I called the crown jewel, and the volume kicker I said would arrive in 2026 through 2028 arrived early and larger than I modelled. In the deep dive, I had A&T shipments growing 6% this year. They are running at +20%.

Management was careful on the call. Asked how much of the $2,083 per tonne is durable, the CEO called it “an exceptional quarter” driven by an extremely strong product mix, and reiterated a through-cycle guide of $1,300 per tonne. The CFO added that the segment has averaged a little above $1,500 per tonne since 2022 and that 2027 should stay at “a high level, not as high as over $2,000.” Those two numbers, $1,300 and $1,500, are the ones I stress the model against later.

P&ARP also set a record up 123%, with EBITDA per tonne up 131%. Costs contributed most of the improvement, followed by price & mix $20M partially offset by volume.

That $74M cost line is the windfall I flagged in the deep dive: wide scrap spreads, favourable metal costs at Muscle Shoals and Neuf-Brisach, and the tariff-inflated US metal environment.

Packaging shipments fell 9%, which reads like demand weakness. It was not. Management diverted rolling capacity away from canstock and into automotive body sheet, which is technically harder and pays better, to cover the North American shortage. Underlying packaging demand was described as healthy in both regions, and the CEO said plainly that as automotive tapers, “we expect to be doing more packaging again.” A 9% volume decline caused by choosing the more profitable product is a different fact from a 9% decline caused by losing customers.

AS&I’s earnings up 44%, and remains the broken corner. Shipments were flat, price and mix was a headwind, and the entire improvement came from a cost tailwind. European automotive demand is still weak, particularly in the premium segment where Constellium is most exposed.

The same competitor outage that handed P&ARP and A&T a windfall hurt AS&I, because some carmakers cut production on platforms that could not get rolled product. The group is a net beneficiary, but the benefit is not evenly distributed.

The TTM view is the cleanest summary of what has happened here. In four quarters, TTM segment profit went from $541M to $982M. P&ARP roughly doubled. Net income went from $34M to $546M. And the market capitalization is $3.8B.

The balance sheet stopped being a story

Net debt fell to and leverage to 1.8x, from 2.2x last quarter and 3.5x a year ago.

That is a full turn and a half of deleveraging in twelve months, achieved on essentially flat net debt, because the denominator grew. Liquidity is $1,058M.

In July, the company redeemed $100M of the 5.625% notes due 2028 early, leaving $225M outstanding, and the next maturity after that is 2029.

FCF was $90M in the quarter and $95M for the half, against a full-year guide now above $300M. That back-loading is normal for this business, since working capital builds in the first half when metal prices rise, and the second half releases it.

On buybacks, the company repurchased 623k shares for $20M in the quarter, summing for a total 1.8 million shares retired in the first half of 2026 for $48M. Since the programme began in 2024, it has retired 15.3 million shares for $241M, at an average price near $15.75, with $287M of authorization left running to December 2028.

Note the pace, though. Q1 was 1.2M shares for $28M; Q2 was 623k for $20M. The company bought less stock as the price rose, which is disciplined and also means less float came out than the headline authorization implies.

I would rather have the discipline.

But if management genuinely believes the shares are worth what I think they are worth, the current price is an argument for accelerating, not slowing.

The scorecard: what I got right, and what I got wrong

Even though the deep dive is 4 weeks old, here is the scorecard so far.

What I got right

  • Guidance was conservative. I wrote that two raises inside a single quarter is what happens when a business inflects faster than its own management expects. Ten weeks later they raised again, to $980M-$1.020B.

  • The 2028 targets were sandbagged. I called them management’s own deliberately conservative targets and priced them at $50 a share. They were delivered in 2026 instead, two years early.

  • Aerospace volume was about to arrive. I wrote that the volume kicker missing from the 2025 margin story arrives in 2026 through 2028. A&T shipments rose 21% in Q2, aerospace 14% and TID 26%.

  • Muscle Shoals and recycling drive P&ARP. I mapped a margin path from 7.0% toward a 9.5% cap on utilization and recycling. The segment printed a record $165M at $621 per tonne.

  • Deleveraging is a re-rating trigger. The model had leverage through 1x by 2028. It reached 1.8x in June, from 3.5x a year earlier, with $100M of the 2028 notes redeemed early on top.

  • AS&I is an option, not a pillar. I wrote that if Europe never recovers the segment stays a rounding error and the thesis survives. It earned $26M on flat volume and negative price and mix, and the thesis survived.

  • A record year would get sold. I wrote that record years in this sector have historically been sold. The stock fell 6% on the best print in company history.

What I got wrong

  • A&T shipment growth. I modelled 6% for 2026. It is running at 20%. I have moved the full year to 18%.

  • 2026 revenue. I modelled 4% growth and held metal flat off the elevated 2025 base. H1 revenue came in 28% higher and the full year is tracking 19%.

  • P&ARP shipment growth. I modelled 3.5%. H1 came in at -3%, because management deliberately switched rolling capacity out of packaging and into automotive body sheet.

  • Tax rate. I used 23% as a normalized French statutory rate. The H1 effective rate was 29.2% and the TTM was 29.6%. This is the miss and I have fixed it for 2026.

Four misses. Three of them are the same miss: I under-forecast volume and I under-forecast metal prices, so my revenue line was below reality. The good news is that a converter’s revenue line is mostly pass-through metal, so being wrong on it costs me very little in value terms; the EBITDA is set by tonnes and conversion margin, not by the LME. The bad news is that it made my margin percentages look better than they should have, and I have now corrected that in the model.

The tax miss is the one that costs real money, and I have fixed it for 2026.

The A&T volume miss is the most interesting. I built a thesis on an aerospace recovery arriving over three years and it substantially arrived in two quarters.

Thesis scorecard after Q2 2026

Pillar #1. A&T, the crown jewel: Confirmed and strengthening

Original thesis: Issoire and Ravenswood are structurally advantaged aerospace plate assets behind a multi-year qualification moat; margin had already improved without volume, and the volume was coming as destocking ended and Airbus and Boeing lifted build rates.

What happened since the deep dive: Record revenue and per tonne. Shipments +21%, with aerospace +14% and TID +26%. Volume and price/mix were the EBITDA contributors. The third Airware cast house at Issoire started up on time and on budget, is in customer qualification now, and ramps through 2027. Management said it expects to be “fully booked for the next several years” in North American automotive and has seen no pricing impact from new entrants.

Assessment: The strongest confirmation in the report, because it came from tonnes rather than spreads. The one caution is that $2,083 per tonne is explicitly not the run rate; management guides $1,300 through cycle and has averaged $1,500 since 2022. My model still assumes A&T earns more per tonne in 2027 than in 2026, which is now the single most aggressive assumption in the build.

Pillar #2. P&ARP, the problem child grown up: Confirmed, windfall-heavy

Original thesis: Muscle Shoals is fixed and setting operational records, the recycling build-out is structural, and the body-sheet position pre-dates the competitor fire and survives it. Margin from 7.0% toward a 9.5% cap.

What happened since the deep dive: Record revenues, +123%, at $621 per tonne. Most of the improvement came via costs, which is where scrap spreads and metal dynamics sit, and volume was negative. Management confirmed Q3 scrap needs are essentially locked and a large portion of Q4 as well, at spreads “similar to the first half,” while guiding the y/y benefit to taper. Neuf-Brisach reaches full recycling capacity in 2027 and the Muscle Shoals cast house comes online in the second half of 2027.

Assessment: Confirmed, with a distinction. The margin got where I said it would get through the windfall channel rather than the structural one. The structural drivers I pointed at are real and still ahead.

Pillar #3. AS&I, the cheap option: Unchanged

Original thesis: A broken segment worth treating as a free option rather than a pillar. If Europe never recovers the thesis survives; if it normalizes there is +$100M of EBITDA nobody is paying for.

What happened since the deep dive: $26M, +44%, entirely from a cost tailwind. Flat shipments, negative price and mix. European premium-segment demand remains weak with Chinese competition intensifying. The segment lost volume on platforms disrupted by the North American rolled-product outage. CSTM sold its Changchun automotive structures JV in China in June.

Assessment: No change. If anything, the strike moved further away: the recovery is later than I assumed a month ago. The Changchun disposal is a small tidy-up of the weakest geography and I read it as mildly positive.

Pillar #4. Capital allocation compounds per-share value: Confirmed and strengthening

Original thesis: Buybacks over dividends, deleveraging into a net cash position, and return-seeking capex at attractive returns inside the fence.

What happened since the deep dive: Leverage 1.8x, inside the 1.5x to 2.5x target and heading lower. $100M of the 2028 notes redeemed early in July, the first voluntary principal reduction in years. 623k shares retired for $20M. Management restated that every project in the return-seeking slate clears a 15% IRR, “and obviously some are more attractive than that.” Energy hedging now covers more than half of 2027 consumption.

Assessment: The most reliable pillar. Early debt redemption while simultaneously buying stock, at 1.8x leverage, is a company that has run out of balance-sheet problems to solve. My only quibble is the slower buyback pace at a lower share price.

Pillar #5. The market is pricing the old company: Confirmed, and the gap widened

Original thesis: A durable earnings base near management’s $900M, worth $60 a share against a $30.11 price, with a $20 bear case and an R/R of 1 to 2.9. Even pricing management’s own windfall-free targets got me $50.

What happened since the deep dive: The durable base assumption was too low. Management now guides $980M to $1.020B and has delivered the 2028 target in 2026. My model output moved to $62. The share price moved from $30.11 to $28.35.

Assessment: On 6 July the setup was $60 against $30.11 with a $20 floor, an R/R of 1 to 2.9. Today it is $62 against $28.35 with the same floor, an R/R of 1 to 4.0. The asymmetry improved by half again in four weeks, and it improved for the right reason: the numerator went up while the denominator went down. Today is a better entry than the one I took.

The guidance raise, and the second half nobody believes

Guidance moved from $900M-$940M to $980M-$1.020B ex metal lag, and FCF from above $275M to above $300M. Capex is unchanged at approximately $330M, cash interest at approximately $125M, and cash taxes rose to approximately $105M on higher profitability. Corporate costs are now guided at approximately $55M for the year.

H1 Segment Adjusted EBITDA was $572M. The new full-year guide of $980M to $1.020B implies a second half of $408M to $448M. That is 22% to 29% below the first half, and at the bottom end it is exactly the $408M the company earned in H2 2025.

Three analysts asked about this on the call, in three different ways. The answers were consistent.

The CEO said that lower European demand in summer and December, and planned maintenance outages concentrated in the second half, which is why H2 always carries higher maintenance cost. She noted that H2 2025 also contained one-off benefits in AS&I in Q3 and an unusually strong Q4 in A&T, making the comparison harder than it looks. Her summary was that the implied first-half to second-half split “is actually very, very close to historic proportion.”

The CFO gave the metal explanation: the recycling environment was adverse in H1 2025, stabilized in Q3 and improved sharply in Q4, so the year-over-year benefit naturally compresses as the comparison base rises.

An analyst then pushed on it directly, pointing out that the low end assumes flat second-half EBITDA y/y despite higher metal prices, a better aerospace outlook, and the Oswego benefit still running in Q3. The CEO’s answered that the low end reflects macro and geopolitical uncertainty, metal and scrap markets that “are moving very, very fast,” and a deliberate choice to sit “in the middle of the road.”

Put that next to the CFO’s disclosure that Q3 scrap volumes are essentially locked and much of Q4 too, at spreads similar to the first half, and the shape of the guide becomes clearer. The primary driver of the H1 windfall is contractually secured for most of the period the guidance covers. Management is not telling you the tailwind stops; it is telling you it will not forecast a tailwind it cannot control.

This is the second raise of 2026. The company guided $780M-$820M in February, took it to $900M-$940M in April, and to $980M-$1.020B in July, a 25% lift to the midpoint in five months. A management team that has run past its own guidance twice and describes its posture as “middle of the road” is telling you something.

The CEO was explicit that the net positive from the North American rolled-product outage “starts to taper off in the third quarter” and normalizes by year-end, and she was careful to add that the returning capacity is not new capacity, just restored capacity covered by existing contracts. That is a real headwind, it is already in the guide.

One thing that is new, and structural

An item came up on the call that was not in the deep dive at all, and it cuts against the central bear argument. The European Commission is considering an export tax on aluminium scrap, with a decision expected in September 2026. The industry association has asked for 30%, which the CEO thinks is unlikely to be granted in full, but she expects some version to pass, taking effect from the beginning of 2027 after member-state ratification. Her assessment: “It’s definitely going to support scrap spreads in Europe and it’s good for our recycling investment in Neuf-Brisach.”

My deep dive treated scrap spreads as a purely mean-reverting windfall. The CFO’s own framing is that recycling economics “have averaged out over time.” If Europe puts a structural tax on scrap exports, that changes for the European half of the business, precisely as the Neuf-Brisach recycling centre reaches full capacity. I am not putting it in the model until it passes. But the possibility that one of my three temporary tailwinds becomes semi-permanent in one geography is a genuine upside I did not have a month ago.

Valuation: what changed in the model

I have rolled the model through Q2 and the new guidance. The rule I set myself was to update 2026 only and leave every outer-year assumption where it was, so that the target moves because of what the company reported. Every changed cell carries a comment explaining the source. You can view the full model here.

The 2026 line

Segment Adjusted EBITDA goes from $920M to $1,002M, a shade above the $1,000M midpoint of the new guidance. Revenue goes from $8.8B to $10.1B, a rise of 19% rather than the 4% I had.

In the model, A&T’s segment margin falls from 19.5% to 17.3%. P&ARP’s goes to 8.7%. AS&I’s drops from 7.0% to 5.7%. Every headline margin percentage in the 2026 column went down.

The reason is that roughly all of a converter’s revenue line is metal it bought and passed straight through to the customer at no margin. When aluminum and the Midwest premium rise, revenue inflates, the denominator grows, and the margin percentage falls even though the company is earning more per tonne on the same work.

A&T’s dollar EBITDA in my 2026 forecast rose from $406M to $427M while its margin percentage fell 220 basis points. Both numbers are correct.

This is why I model this business in dollars per tonne and only convert to percentages at the end, and it is why any screen that ranks aluminium converters on EBITDA margin is measuring the aluminium price.

Three other 2026 inputs changed:

  • Tax rate 23% to 29%. My normalized French statutory assumption was wrong for the current year. The H1 effective rate was 29.2% and the trailing twelve months 29.6%. I have left 23% in place from 2027 onward. If the French surtax persists, the outer years are too generous as well.

  • D&A 3.9% to 3.4% of revenue. Dollar depreciation is unchanged near $338M; only the denominator moved.

  • Capex intensity 3.7% to 3.3%. Same story. Management reiterated approximately $330M of capex including roughly $100M of return-seeking spend at Issoire, Muscle Shoals and Ravenswood.

What I deliberately did not change

2027 and everything beyond it is untouched. On the new base, the model produces $996M of Segment Adjusted EBITDA in 2027 against the $981M it produced before, so the outer years are effectively where they were. The forecast now shows 2026 at $1,002M and 2027 at $996M, a flat year rather than a growth year.

That flatness is deliberate. The model also carries a 2027 revenue decline of about 10%, because unit prices from 2027 onward assume metal normalizes off the current tariff-inflated base rather than compounding from it. If metal stays where it is, that line is too conservative and both revenue and working capital are understated.

Stressing the most aggressive assumption

Pillar #1 flagged it: my model has A&T earning $1,865 per tonne in 2027, above the $1,750 it implies for 2026, and well above the $1,300 through-cycle figure management guides and the $1,500 average the CFO cited for the period since 2022. That is the assumption most likely to be wrong, so I ran it two ways.

  • Set 2027 A&T to management’s $1,500 per tonne average, cutting that year’s segment profit by $94M. The target moves from $62.80 to $61.70. One year of fade, discounted, barely registers.

  • Also cut the long-run A&T margin cap from 20% to 17%, permanently, for every year to 2037. The target falls to $54.90.

The second case is the one that matters. A single soft year is noise in a ten-year model, while a permanently lower ceiling costs $8 a share. Even in that case, with the segment I called the crown jewel permanently downgraded, the model still says the shares are worth nearly double today’s price.

Risk register update

Materialized

The automotive supply windfall is ending, on schedule. Management confirmed the North American benefit tapers from Q3 and normalizes by year-end as the competitor’s capacity returns. I called this in the deep dive. The offset is that the returning tonnes are covered by pre-existing contracts, so this is a return to normal rather than a share loss.

A record year did get sold. I wrote that record years in this sector have historically been sold, and the stock fell 6% on the best print in company history.

Faded

The scrap-spread cliff, at least through 2026. The bear case assumed spreads mean-revert. CSTM has locked essentially all of Q3 and much of Q4 at spreads similar to H1. The tailwind cannot vanish inside this year, whatever the spot market does. The 2027 question is untouched by any of that and stays live: the $74M cost tailwind in Q2 is the number that has to be replaced next year, and only part of it has a named structural successor in Neuf-Brisach, the Muscle Shoals cast house and a possible EU export tax. That is the central open risk on the thesis and the reason I did not raise the outer years.

Balance-sheet fragility. At 1.8x with $1,058M of liquidity, nothing due before 2028, and $100M of that 2028 maturity already retired, the debt argument no longer carries weight. I am retiring it from the register.

Unchanged

European automotive. Still weak, still the reason AS&I is an option rather than a pillar, still the largest structural drag on the group.

Customer concentration. The top ten remain over half of revenue with two customers each above 10%.

Aerospace timing. Less acute after a +21% shipment quarter, but the build-rate ramp still depends on Airbus and Boeing hitting rates they have missed before. Management sees no restocking yet, only higher purchase rates matching higher build rates, which is the healthier of the two explanations.

New

The 2027 A&T reversion. Q2’s $2,083 per tonne is explicitly not a run rate. If the segment reverts to management’s $1,300 through-cycle guide rather than settling in the $1,500 to $1,900 band my model assumes, its most valuable segment is materially over-earning in the forecast. Sized above at $8 a share if the reversion is permanent.

Tax. The 29% effective rate is 600 basis points above the normalized assumption I carry from 2027. A French tax examination opened in February 2026 and remains open.

Middle East cost inflation. Management flagged emerging pressure in freight, lubricants and coatings, and sources some slab and billet from the region. It called the impact digestible and most 2026 energy is hedged, with over half of 2027 consumption already locked.

Guidance credibility, in the other direction. Two raises in five months is a strong record, but it also means the shares now carry an expectation of raises. A quarter that merely meets guidance would be read as a miss.

Where the company sits against its peers

Against a ten-name materials peer set, CSTM carries the highest composite score in the group at 91.7. More useful than the ranking is the shape of it. CSTM has no weak factor: its lowest score of the five is Growth at 61.6. Every other name in the table has at least one factor in the thirties or below, and the next-best floor belongs to Kaiser Aluminum [] at 41.8. Century Aluminum [] scores 95.6 on Growth and 38.8 on Valuation. Materion [] scores 88.0 on Growth and 8.8 on Valuation. Ero Copper [] is the closest analogue on cheapness and profitability, at 69.7 and 90.9, and then scores 29.0 on Outlook. DRDGOLD [] scores 98.4 on Profitability and 24.9 on Sentiment.

The plain reading is that within its own sector this is the rare name with no obvious hole in it.

On price, though, I had this wrong when I started writing. This is not a stock-specific derating. Since the deep dive on 6 July, CSTM is down 8.0%, and most of the peer set is down with it: Materion -19.5%, Kaiser -10.8%, Century -4.1%, Ero Copper -0.5%. CSTM sits in the middle of that pack, not at the bottom of it.

The common cause is easy to name. Sell-side aluminium price forecasts were cut through July on the view that the metal, the US Midwest premium and scrap spreads all normalise into the second half and 2027, and the whole downstream complex was marked down on it. Kaiser is the cleanest illustration: it reported on 22 July with adjusted EPS of $5.53 against a $2.66 consensus, more than doubling the estimate, and lifted its full-year EBITDA growth guidance from 20-30% to 45-55%. Its shares still sit 19% below their 52-week high. Century, which has not even reported yet, is 36% below its own high while a US Commerce Secretary tours its expanded smelter.

So the market is not making a judgement about CSTM but rather about 2027 aluminum, and applying it uniformly to everything that converts the metal.

Verdict

Maintaining BUY, raising the target from $60 to $62, bear case unchanged at $20. At $28.35 that is an R/R of 1 to 4.0, up from 1 to 2.9 at the deep dive four weeks ago.

Here is the thought I would leave you with.

Management just pulled its 2028 targets forward into 2026, and the stock went down. What I find hard to argue with is the arithmetic on the other side. Discount my numbers at 11%, strip out terminal growth entirely, and the model still lands above today’s price. You do not need the aerospace ramp, the Neuf-Brisach recycling centre, the Airware cast house or a European scrap tax to justify the shares. Those are all free. What you need is for a company earning $982M on a trailing basis, at 1.8x leverage, to not fall apart.

If this changed how you think about the difference between a record and a peak, share it with someone who owns cyclicals.
